cards.title: FO model checking on hereditary monadically dependent graph classes
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
For every hereditary effectively monadically dependent class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, is first-order model checking fixed-parameter tractable with a computable parameter dependence?

Precisely, does every such \(\mathcal C\) admit a single deterministic algorithm \(A_{\mathcal C}\), a total computable function \(f_{\mathcal C}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and a constant integer \(d_{\mathcal C}\ge0\) such that, for every \(G\in\mathcal C\) and every first-order graph sentence \(\varphi\), the algorithm outputs whether \(G\models\varphi\) within
\[f_{\mathcal C}(|\varphi|)\,(|V(G)|+1)^{d_{\mathcal C}}\]
steps? The algorithm receives only the graph and the sentence, in the encodings below, and must halt on every input. The exponent may depend on the class but not on the sentence. The effective structural hypothesis is the computable powerset-obstruction bound defined below.
cards.definitions:
Graph class and promise. A finite simple undirected graph has a finite vertex set and a symmetric irreflexive adjacency relation \(E\); the empty graph is permitted. A class \(\mathcal C\) is closed under graph isomorphism. It is hereditary if \(G[S]\in\mathcal C\) for every \(G\in\mathcal C\) and every \(S\subseteq V(G)\), where \(G[S]\) retains exactly the edges with both endpoints in \(S\). The class is fixed before the algorithm is chosen, not given as part of an instance. No decision procedure for membership in the class is assumed. Correctness and the displayed time bound are required only when the input graph belongs to the class. On other inputs the algorithm may return either answer, but must halt.

First-order syntax and truth. The graph signature has equality and a binary adjacency symbol, with variables \(x_i\) indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\). Formulas are built from atoms \(x_i=x_j\), \(E(x_i,x_j)\), negation, binary conjunction, and existential quantification \(\exists x_i\); other connectives and universal quantification are abbreviations expanded into this syntax. A sentence has no free variables. Atoms are interpreted using actual equality and graph adjacency; Boolean operations have their usual truth tables, and quantifiers range over all vertices. On the empty graph an existential statement is false and a universal statement is true. The query language has no unary predicates, vertex order, arithmetic, function symbols or set quantification. Write \(G\models\varphi\) for truth of the sentence.

Encoding and computation. For a nonnegative integer \(i\), let \(\ell\) be the binary length of \(i+1\), and encode it as \(U(i)=1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(i+1)\), where the last part has exactly \(\ell\) bits. Encode \(G\) with labeled vertex set \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) as \(U(n)\) followed by its upper-triangular adjacency bits, in lexicographic order of pairs \(i<j\). All these bits are supplied explicitly. Formulas use prefix syntax: tags 000, 001, 010, 011, 100 respectively stand for equality, adjacency, negation, conjunction and existential quantification. An atom tag is followed by \(U(i)U(j)\), negation by one encoded subformula, conjunction by two in order, and the existential tag by \(U(i)\) and one subformula. The parameter \(|\varphi|\) is this binary length, including variable indices. A valid input concatenates the graph code and one sentence code; invalid inputs may be rejected. An algorithm is a finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite tape alphabet and no oracle, advice or randomness; time counts its transitions. Polynomial simulation overhead between the usual explicit graph representations and finite-word computational models can be absorbed in the class-dependent exponent and parameter function.

Unary expansions for the structural condition. For this purpose only, allow additional unary symbols \(P_j\), \(j\in\mathbb N\), with atom \(P_j(x_i)\) encoded by tag 101 followed by \(U(j)U(i)\). Each formula uses finitely many such symbols. They are interpreted independently as arbitrary vertex subsets; they may overlap. Their names and variable indices are included in formula length. There are no additional parameters or constant symbols.

Transduction. Let \(\theta(x_0,x_1)\) be any formula in this expanded syntax whose only possible free variables are \(x_0,x_1\). Given \(G\), choose arbitrary interpretations of all unary symbols used in \(\theta\). On the same vertex set, form an undirected graph by putting an edge between distinct \(u,v\) exactly when \(\theta(u,v)\lor\theta(v,u)\) holds in that expansion of \(G\). Finally keep any subset of vertices and take the induced graph on it. Denote by \(T_\theta(G)\) the set of all graphs obtainable in this way, up to isomorphism. Colors are discarded in the output. There is no copying of vertices or tuple-valued output domain in this definition.

Monadic dependence and its effective version. A class is monadically dependent when no single formula \(\theta\) produces every finite simple graph among the outputs \(T_\theta(G)\) as \(G\) ranges over the class. To state the quantitative promise, for an integer \(s\ge1\) let \(P_s\) be the bipartite powerset graph with disjoint vertex sets \(\{a_1,\ldots,a_s\}\) and \(\{b_S:S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,s\}\}\), and edges exactly \(a_i b_S\) with \(i\in S\). It has \(s+2^s\) vertices and no edges within either part.

The class \(\mathcal C\) is effectively monadically dependent if there is a total computable function \(b:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that
\[\forall\theta\ \forall G\in\mathcal C:\quad P_{b(|\theta|)}\notin T_\theta(G).\]
Absence means that no choice of unary predicates and retained vertex subset yields a graph isomorphic to that powerset graph. The bound is uniform over all formulas of the given length, all graphs in the class, and all their colorings. It is the effective dependence-function convention of Mählmann’s Definition 12.24, which in particular implies monadic dependence. The finite program computing \(b\) may depend on \(\mathcal C\).

Uniformity of the requested algorithm. For each class, one finite program \(A_{\mathcal C}\) must handle all input sentence lengths. It may depend on the class and its effective dependence witness, but receives neither a class-membership certificate nor a graph decomposition on an instance. The quantifiers are class-wise existence of the algorithm, computable function and exponent; no single procedure that accepts arbitrary descriptions of classes and constructs their algorithms is required. There is no prescribed growth rate for \(f_{\mathcal C}\), beyond total computability.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish, for every class satisfying the hereditary and effective-dependence promises, one total deterministic algorithm and one computable parameter bound with a sentence-independent polynomial exponent, for the specified graph-and-sentence input model.

A negative answer must establish a particular hereditary effectively monadically dependent class for which no such algorithm, computable parameter function and fixed exponent work. In particular, every candidate total deterministic algorithm and bound must fail on some graph in that class and some sentence, either in correctness or in running time. An obstruction applying only to one proposed algorithm, an ineffective class, or a restricted decomposition method is insufficient. A conditional hardness result alone does not refute this unconditional target unless its additional assumption is also proved. Structural existence theorems, a different algorithm for each sentence length, randomized algorithms, or algorithms supplied with extra decompositions do not by themselves meet the criterion.
cards.why: First-order formulas express a broad family of graph queries, but direct evaluation lets the graph-size exponent grow with the query. The proposed structural condition aims to explain when that dependence can be confined to a computable function of the query alone, even on dense graph classes. Settling this tractability direction would complement the established hardness of hereditary classes that can logically encode arbitrary graphs.

importance.reason: The central proposed tractability boundary for first-order model checking on hereditary graph classes, connecting database queries, model theory, sparsity and dense graph structure.

progress.text: First-order model checking is established for monadically stable classes; effective parameter bounds are treated explicitly in the dissertation.
The flip-breakability paper proves the hardness direction on every hereditary monadically independent class.
The dissertation distinguishes computable obstruction and runtime bounds in Definition 12.24 and Theorem 12.25.
Merge-width yields a general model-checking theorem with a supplied witnessing construction sequence.
Randomized faster ordering and cover algorithms improve the monadically stable model-checking application.

Almost linear neighborhood complexity and polynomial-time radius-one merge-width constructions are proved for all monadically dependent classes; the full tractability conjecture remains explicitly open.

context_blocks.text: First-order model checking asks whether a finite graph satisfies an input sentence. Clique, independent-set and dominating-set queries of a specified size are basic examples. Trying all assignments of vertices to variables gives polynomial time for each fixed sentence, but its exponent depends on the sentence. Fixed-parameter tractability requires one exponent for all sentences on the chosen class.

For example, a sentence can assert the existence of a fixed number of vertices such that every other vertex is adjacent to at least one of them. Increasing that number increases the sentence length and the direct enumeration cost. The target permits an arbitrarily large computable cost depending on sentence length, while keeping a fixed polynomial dependence on the graph size. It is a uniform guarantee across the whole query language.

The hereditary condition is closure under deleting vertices, keeping all remaining edges. It allows sparse and dense classes alike. Complete graphs illustrate why edge density is not itself the barrier: a dense class may still have tightly controlled logical behavior. The conjectured boundary uses what a fixed formula can encode after arbitrary unary marking, rather than an edge-count bound.

A transduction changes the edge relation according to a formula, after vertices have been marked by finitely many unary predicates, and may discard vertices. The formula is fixed while graph size grows. Monadic independence means that one such fixed scheme can yield every finite graph. Dependence excludes this unrestricted encoding, while allowing richer structure than monadic stability.

Computability is a genuine qualification in the saved target. A class can have a finite obstruction bound at each formula length without any computable function dominating those bounds. The dissertation illustrates this distinction with graph classes indexed by Busy Beaver growth. That example shows why a proof with arbitrary class-dependent constants cannot automatically be advertised as a computable FPT bound; it is not itself an unconditional counterexample to the present effective conjecture.

The structural witness and the query algorithm play different roles. The function b bounds powerset graphs obtainable by all short colored formulas; it does not recognize which graphs belong to the class. The requested algorithm receives a promised member of the class and an uncolored sentence. Neither a membership test nor a decomposition oracle is included in the input.

Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk prove that model checking is \(\mathrm{AW}[*]\)-hard on every hereditary monadically independent class. Their stronger interpretation theorem produces uncolored instances efficiently, so this is not merely a hardness statement with extra vertex colors supplied. Under the standard assumption \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne\mathrm{AW}[*]\), the independent side cannot have FPT model checking. That conditional intractability does not prove the positive dependent side.

Monadic stability is the stronger condition excluding arbitrarily large half-graphs under transductions: a half-graph of order \(s\) has two disjoint parts \(a_1,\ldots,a_s\) and \(b_1,\ldots,b_s\), with edge \(a_i b_j\) exactly when \(i\le j\). The stable-class model-checking theorem gives a major positive case. The dissertation makes its parameter function computable under effective stability bounds; ordinary stability alone should not silently be substituted for that effective hypothesis.

Merge-width measures graph construction sequences that merge vertex groups and resolve pairs as edges or nonedges. At radius r, the width bounds how many current groups a vertex can reach using at most r resolved pairs. The existing bounded-merge-width model-checking theorem assumes that a witnessing sequence is supplied. Existence of a useful sequence alone does not meet the card’s input model.

The July 2026 paper proves almost linear neighborhood complexity for every monadically dependent class. Writing \(N_G(v)\) for the neighbors of \(v\), for every \(\eta>0\) there is a constant \(c_{\mathcal C,\eta}\) such that for all \(G\in\mathcal C\) and all nonempty \(S\subseteq V(G)\), the number of distinct sets \(N_G(v)\cap S\) is at most \(c_{\mathcal C,\eta}|S|^{1+\eta}\). The nonempty-set qualification avoids the zero-size edge case.

The same paper constructs radius-one merge-width sequences in \(O(n^5)\) time, with width \(n^{o(1)}\) on every monadically dependent class. Here \(n^{o(1)}\) means that for every fixed positive exponent the width is eventually at most a constant times that power of \(n\), with constants depending on the class. This is meaningful algorithmic progress, but gives neither a constant width bound nor corresponding control at all larger radii.

Dreier and Kuske’s February 2026 work speeds up low-crossing orders and neighborhood covers, with a faster model-checking application for monadically stable classes. Its ordering and cover subroutines use randomness. A faster theorem on that already understood subclass does not establish the deterministic guarantee for every effectively monadically dependent class.

The July 2026 paper explicitly retains the general tractability direction as open. A positive answer here would establish the effective algorithmic direction of the proposed classification. A negative answer would require an effective hereditary class that defeats every single uniform algorithm with computable parameter dependence, not merely a class whose currently known decomposition bounds are ineffective.

sentences: First-order model checking evaluates a vertex-quantified logical sentence on an explicitly given finite graph.

The question asks for a uniform deterministic algorithm on each hereditary effectively monadically dependent class, with computable parameter dependence and a sentence-independent graph-size exponent.
Effective monadic dependence bounds the powerset graphs obtainable through short formulas with arbitrary unary vertex markings.
The algorithm receives no graph decomposition or class-membership certificate, and must work for all sentences on its fixed class.
Hereditary independent classes have a hardness theorem and effectively stable classes have algorithms, while the July 2026 radius-one results leave the full positive direction open.

source_formulation.text: Preserves importance 96 and the already selected effective, class-wise deterministic FPT formulation for plain graph sentences. The computable powerset-obstruction convention is explicitly grounded in Mählmann Definition12.24; the general survey deliberately suppresses such computability qualifications. This review fixes concrete finite encodings and time semantics without imposing an exponent uniform over all classes, a class-recognition algorithm, a supplied decomposition or colored per-instance query input. Different reasonable syntax encodings transfer computable structural bounds effectively.

checked_sources: Read full Mählmann dissertation Chapter 4, including powerset graph definition, transduction conventions and Corollary 4.8; §12.4 printed pp.157–159, Example 12.23, Definition 12.24 and Theorem 12.25. Exact effective definition forbids the powerset graph of order b(|theta|) in T_theta(G). The stable theorem obtains a computable parameter dependence under effective monadic stability. The Busy Beaver example concerns ineffective structural bounds, not a proved unconditional refutation of all possible model-checking algorithms.

Read Pilipczuk arXiv:2501.04166 §2.2, footnote2, §2.3 and Conjecture 2. The survey explicitly brushes computable-parameter issues aside, so its broad FPT wording is not used to erase the card’s effective hypothesis. The class-dependent exponent convention is retained.

Read arXiv:2403.15201v2 introduction, Conjecture 1.1 and Theorems 1.3, 1.6–1.8. Theorem 1.8 efficiently interprets all graphs without a nondeterministic coloring step in hereditary independent classes, supporting the plain-graph hardness statement. Primary metadata confirms 27 March 2024 revision. Did not reuse a secondary generated page’s incorrect later attribution.

Read full arXiv:2311.18740 introduction and Theorem 1, then the dissertation’s explicit effectiveness treatment rather than inferring computability from big-O subscripts. The already tractable stable subclass is not identified with the full dependent class.

Read arXiv:2502.18065v2, revised 23 June 2026, introduction and supplied-construction-sequence model-checking statement. Verified the radius-indexed definition and distinction between bounded and almost bounded merge-width. A decomposition assumed on input is not automatically computable from the graph in the required time.

Read arXiv:2602.14625v1 full introduction, Theorems 1.2–1.5 and Corollary 1.6. Ordering/cover guarantees are randomized, with success probability 2/3 in the stated subroutines; the faster FO application is still for monadically stable classes. Did not assert deterministic general dependent-class tractability from this paper.

Read arXiv:2607.10941v1 full introduction, Conjecture 1, Theorems 2, 4, 5, §2 transduction definitions and §3 construction-sequence definition. Verified explicit open tractability direction, almost linear neighborhood traces on nonempty subsets and O(n^5) radius-one construction with O(n^(1−1/d) log n) width under a c|S|^d trace bound. Corrected the empty-set edge case instead of reproducing informal asymptotic notation literally.

Bounded later searches through 16 September 2026, including August/September arXiv identifiers, found no inspected general resolution. Primary abstract of arXiv:2606.18934 concerns extra antisymmetric relations, bounded-independence expansions and selected oriented classes; SoCG2026.51 concerns particular geometric classes. These were scope checks, not independent proof audits. Secondary generated summaries and future-dated journal issue labels were not used as general-resolution evidence.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
